stances.claim: By end of his six-year term, Duterte will have named 11 of 15 Supreme Court justices — a constitutional reshaping of the Court's profile that is unprecedented in recent PH history and carries profound long-term implications for jurisprudence.
stances.rhetorical_move: arithmetic-projection argument presenting the retirement schedule as a structural fact, not a political critique

stances.claim: The De Castro vs JBC ruling (9-3) permitting midnight SC appointments — which allowed GMA to appoint Corona — remains binding precedent and will authorize Duterte to fill the Peralta and Bernabe vacancies in 2022 even within the pre-election ban window.
stances.rhetorical_move: precedent-application analysis identifying the constitutional tension and its existing judicial resolution

stances.claim: The Court's growing career-jurist composition (all four Duterte appointees from CA/Sandiganbayan) signals a shift away from the prior practice of appointing private practitioners directly to the bench.
stances.rhetorical_move: profile-observation without explicit normative judgment (neutral descriptive framing with 'career jurists are happy' as indirect endorsement)

notable_anecdotes: The arithmetic puzzle of why Duterte gets 11 appointments despite filling only 4 so far — resolved by the fact that three of his own first four appointees will themselves retire within his term, creating replacement slots; CJ uses this as an accessible explainer to demystify a counterintuitive constitutional arithmetic.
The law school breakdown of all 15 sitting justices (UP 6, Ateneo 5, San Beda 2, UST 1, UE 1) — a rare sociological profile of the Court that is usually undisclosed in mainstream commentary.

The disclosure that more than 80% of all SC cases are decided by divisions (not en banc), and that even a 3-vote division decision is deemed a decision of the entire 15-member Court — a structural fact that most lay readers are unaware of.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban maps all 11 remaining Supreme Court vacancies that President Duterte can fill before his term ends June 30, 2022, explaining the counterintuitive arithmetic: though Duterte has already appointed four justices, three of those four (Martires, Tijam, Reyes) will themselves hit compulsory retirement age of 70 within his term and require replacement. He lists the full retirement chronology -- 2 slots in 2018 (Velasco, De Castro), 6 in 2019 (Martires, Tijam, Del Castillo, Jardeleza, Bersamin, Carpio), 1 in 2020 (Reyes), and 2 in 2022 (Peralta, Bernabe) -- and flags that the 2022 slots fall within the Art. VII Sec. 15 midnight-appointments ban, noting that the SC's 9-3 ruling in De Castro vs JBC (2010) established that this ban does not apply to SC vacancies, a precedent that allowed GMA to appoint Corona and will similarly apply to Duterte. The column also profiles the current 15-member bench by career origin (CA, Sandiganbayan, private practice) and law school (UP 6, Ateneo 5, San Beda 2, UST 1, UE 1), notes that all four Duterte appointees are career jurists, discloses the three newly reorganized divisions, and reminds readers that 80%+ of cases are decided by divisions where even three votes constitute a Court decision.
